Question 1: Bias-Variance Trade-Off Simulation

Two critical tuning parameters of random forests are terminal node size (nmin) and the candidate predictor subset size (mtry). This question conducts a 100-repetition simulation study to empirically assess their impact on the squared bias and variance of predicted values.

The data-generating process comprises \(p = 5\) jointly normal predictors with mean vector \(\boldsymbol{\mu} = \mathbf{0}\) and covariance matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma} \in \mathbb{R}^{5 \times 5}\) satisfying \(\text{Var}(X_j) = 1\) and \(\text{Cor}(X_j, X_k) = 0.3\) for all \(j \neq k\). The scalar response is \[ Y = X_1 + X_3 + X_5 + \varepsilon, \qquad \varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1), \] where the noise \(\varepsilon\) is independent of the predictors. Thus, the true regression function is linear in the active predictors: \[ f(\mathbf{x}) = x_1 + x_3 + x_5, \] while \(X_2\) and \(X_4\) are uninformative noise predictors.

1a. Simulation Setup and Numerical Results

A fixed test set of \(N_{\text{test}} = 200\) predictor vectors was generated once from \(\mathcal{N}_5(\mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma})\) using pseudo-random seed 432 and held constant across all repetitions. The true target values \(f(\mathbf{x}_j) = x_{j,1} + x_{j,3} + x_{j,5}\) were evaluated once for all test points. Across \(R = 100\) independent simulation repetitions:

  1. An independent training set of \(N_{\text{train}} = 200\) observations was generated from the joint distribution \((\mathbf{X}, Y)\).
  2. The exact same training dataset was used to fit all tuning settings within each repetition.
  3. Forests were grown to 500 trees (ntrees = 500), drawing a bootstrap sample of 200 observations with replacement for each tree (replacement = TRUE, resample.prob = 1.0, reinforcement = FALSE). All other fitting parameters remained at their package defaults.
  4. Test predictions \(\hat{f}_r(\mathbf{x}_j)\) were recorded across test points \(j = 1, \dots, 200\) and repetitions \(r = 1, \dots, 100\).

For each setting, the pointwise squared bias and variance were estimated as: \[ \widehat{\text{Bias}}^2(\mathbf{x}_j) = \left( \frac{1}{R} \sum_{r=1}^R \hat{f}_r(\mathbf{x}_j) - f(\mathbf{x}_j) \right)^2, \qquad \widehat{\text{Var}}(\mathbf{x}_j) = \frac{1}{R-1} \sum_{r=1}^R \left( \hat{f}_r(\mathbf{x}_j) - \bar{\hat{f}}(\mathbf{x}_j) \right)^2, \] and subsequently averaged over the \(N_{\text{test}} = 200\) fixed test points: \[ \overline{\text{Bias}^2} = \frac{1}{200} \sum_{j=1}^{200} \widehat{\text{Bias}}^2(\mathbf{x}_j), \qquad \overline{\text{Var}} = \frac{1}{200} \sum_{j=1}^{200} \widehat{\text{Var}}(\mathbf{x}_j), \qquad \overline{\text{MSE}} = \overline{\text{Bias}^2} + \overline{\text{Var}}. \]

Comparison 1: Varying Node Size (nmin) with mtry = 3 Fixed

Fixing mtry = 3, we vary terminal node size nmin \(\in \{1, 5, 10, 20, 30\}\). Table 1 reports the averaged metrics across the 200 test points, and Figure 1 illustrates the bias-variance trade-off curve.

1b. Discussion of the Bias-Variance Trade-Off

1. How does a large node size, such as 30, affect the fit in this example?

The node size parameter (nmin) determines the stopping rule for recursive partitioning: nodes containing at most nmin observations are not split further. As nmin increases from 1 to 30:

  • Substantial Increase in Squared Bias: At nmin = 1, the averaged squared bias is 0.3157. When nmin is increased to 30, squared bias nearly doubles, rising to 0.6054 (+91.8%). A large node size forces trees to terminate early at shallow depths, partitioning the predictor space into very broad geometric cells. Averaging the training responses across these large regions smooths out the genuine linear gradient \(x_1 + x_3 + x_5\), inducing severe underfitting.
  • Modest Reduction in Variance: Concurrently, the variance decreases monotonically from 0.1056 at nmin = 1 down to 0.0525 at nmin = 30 (−50.3%). Larger terminal nodes average over more training observations, dampening the sensitivity of individual leaf predictions to training noise \(\varepsilon\).
  • Net Degradation in Total MSE: Because the increase in squared bias (+0.2897) far exceeds the variance reduction (−0.0531), the overall prediction MSE deteriorates from its minimum of 0.4165 (at nmin = 5) to 0.6579 at nmin = 30 (+58.0%). In this additive linear regression setting, over-regularizing terminal leaf size severely hurts predictive performance.

2. What are the benefits and drawbacks of using a large mtry value?

  • Benefits of Large mtry (Dramatic Bias Reduction): In this model, only 3 of the 5 predictors (\(X_1, X_3, X_5\)) carry true signal, while \(X_2\) and \(X_4\) are pure noise. When mtry = 1, every split must use whatever single variable is randomly selected. In 40% of splits, an uninformative noise variable is chosen, and in the remaining 60%, only one active variable is available without the ability to optimize split choice. This generates weak, poorly oriented splits, resulting in an enormous squared bias (0.9068). As mtry increases to 5, every split can evaluate all active predictors, enabling trees to reliably split on the most informative features and slashing squared bias by 67.6% down to 0.2935.
  • Drawbacks of Large mtry (Variance Inflation via Tree Correlation): The variance of a random forest ensemble of \(B\) trees is: \[ \text{Var}(\hat{f}_{\text{RF}}(\mathbf{x})) = \rho(\mathbf{x}) \sigma^2(\mathbf{x}) + \frac{1 - \rho(\mathbf{x})}{B} \sigma^2(\mathbf{x}), \] where \(\sigma^2(\mathbf{x})\) is the variance of a single tree and \(\rho(\mathbf{x})\) is the pairwise correlation between trees. When mtry is large, individual trees repeatedly select the same dominant features (\(X_1, X_3, X_5\)) at top-level splits. This causes the trees to become highly correlated (\(\rho \to 1\)), drastically limiting the ensemble's ability to average out estimation errors. As a result, ensemble variance rises from 0.0362 at mtry = 1 to 0.1066 at mtry = 5 (+194.8%).
  • Net Trade-Off: Because the linear additive signal is strong across three predictors, the massive reduction in squared bias (−0.6133) comfortably outweighs the variance inflation (+0.0704), driving total MSE down from 0.9430 at mtry = 1 to 0.4000 at mtry = 5. In problems with many noise predictors or complex nonlinear interactions, intermediate values of mtry (e.g. \(\lfloor \sqrt{p} \rfloor\) or \(p/3\)) typically strike the best balance.

3. If each tree instead sampled 100 observations with replacement, would you expect the preferred node size to shift toward smaller or larger values?

When each tree draws a bootstrap sample of only \(n_{\text{sub}} = 100\) observations instead of 200:

  1. Shallower Trees Accelerate Bias Inflation: With only 100 observations per tree, sample mass at each split is halved. If a large node size such as nmin = 20 or 30 is retained, trees can execute at most 2 or 3 splits before terminal node sizes fall below nmin. This causes premature termination, flattening tree depth and causing squared bias to spike sharply (reaching 0.9979 at nmin = 30).
  2. Subsampling Reduces Tree Correlation: Drawing smaller subsamples of 100 observations with replacement injects additional randomization, lowering pairwise tree overlap and reducing between-tree correlation \(\rho\). Consequently, forest variance is naturally low (ranging from 0.0776 at nmin = 1 to 0.0398 at nmin = 30).
  3. Shift to Smaller Preferred Node Size: Because variance is already well-controlled by subsampling, the dominant contributor to overall error becomes squared bias. To allow the shallower trees to capture adequate function complexity, trees must be allowed to split deeper by adopting smaller terminal node sizes.

To confirm this reasoning, we ran an additional simulation across 100 repetitions with \(n_{\text{sub}} = 100\) observations sampled with replacement per tree (resample.prob = 0.5 in RLT). Table 3 and Figure 3 report the empirical results:

Table 3: Additional Simulation — Subsampling 100 Observations with Replacement per Tree (mtry = 3, 100 repetitions)
Node Size (nmin) Averaged Squared Bias Averaged Variance Averaged Total MSE
1  ★ (Minimum MSE)0.42110.07760.4987
50.43770.06580.5035
100.52390.05370.5776
200.75350.04340.7968
300.99790.03981.0377
Figure 3: Total MSE comparison across node size settings between full bootstrap (200 observations) and subsampling (100 observations). The optimal node size shifts from nmin = 5 to nmin = 1.

Conclusion: With full bootstrap sampling (\(N = 200\)), the preferred node size is nmin = 5 (MSE = 0.4165). When sampling 100 observations per tree, the preferred node size shifts toward smaller values, reaching its minimum at nmin = 1 (MSE = 0.4987). This confirms that smaller tree training sample sizes shift the preferred node size toward smaller values to combat premature stopping and excessive bias.

Question 2: Tuning Random Forests for MNIST

We analyze mnist-first2000.csv.gz, which contains 2,000 MNIST observations across 784 pixel features and digit labels:

  • Data Splitting: From the first 1,000 observations, digits 1, 6, and 7 were retained as the training set (\(N_{\text{train}} = 327\), containing 116 ones, 94 sixes, and 117 sevens). From the remaining 1,000 observations, digits 1, 6, and 7 formed the test set (\(N_{\text{test}} = 317\), containing 104 ones, 106 sixes, and 107 sevens).
  • PCA Preprocessing: Principal Component Analysis was fitted strictly to the training pixel matrix, centering pixels by their training means without scaling (prcomp(train_pixels, center = TRUE, scale. = FALSE)). The first 20 principal components were extracted as predictors. Test observations were projected using the identical training means and loadings: \(\mathbf{X}_{\text{test}} = (\mathbf{X}_{\text{test, raw}} - \bar{\mathbf{x}}_{\text{train}}) \mathbf{V}_{20}\).
  • Forest Architecture: RLT classification forests with 1,000 trees (ntrees = 1000), drawing bootstrap samples of size \(N = 327\) with replacement (replacement = TRUE, resample.prob = 1.0, reinforcement = FALSE).

2a. Default Model Fit and OOB Misclassification Rate

The default parameters in RLT are: \[ \text{mtry} = \max\left(1, \lfloor p/3 \rfloor\right) = \lfloor 20/3 \rfloor = 6, \qquad \text{nmin} = \max\left(1, \lfloor \log(N_{\text{train}}) \rfloor\right) = \lfloor \log(327) \rfloor = 5. \] We report both the ensemble out-of-bag (OOB) misclassification rate and the tree-average OOB error rate:

  • Ensemble OOB Misclassification Rate: 0.0306 (3.06%; only 10 errors out of 327 training instances).
  • Tree-Average OOB Error Rate: 0.1963 (19.63%).

The ensemble OOB misclassification rate aggregates the majority vote of all trees for which an observation was out-of-bag. Ensembling reduces individual tree error rates from ~19.6% down to ~3.1% through variance reduction.

However, its ensemble OOB error is 0.0336 (nearly twice as many misclassifications) because setting mtry = 20 forces all trees to choose identical splits, eliminating ensemble diversity. The ensemble OOB rate directly evaluates the actual voting classifier.

Commentary on Results:

  • Dominance of PC2 and PC1: PC2 (importance = 0.4506) and PC1 (importance = 0.3261) exhibit massive importance compared to all other components. In handwritten digits, PC1 and PC2 capture the fundamental geometric distinctions between digits 1, 6, and 7: overall stroke elongation and thin aspect ratio (isolating digit 1), lower circular loop presence (isolating digit 6), and horizontal top-stroke with diagonal stem (isolating digit 7).
  • Secondary Components (PCs 3–7): PC5 (0.0950), PC6 (0.0899), PC3 (0.0881), and PC7 (0.0664) provide crucial secondary discriminatory information for resolving ambiguous cases, such as tilted ones that resemble sevens or sixes with closed top loops.
  • Tail Components (PCs 8–20): Principal components 8 through 20 carry small importance scores (< 0.05), indicating that localized pixel variations and high-frequency noise contribute very little to classifying these digits.
  • Why Small mtry = 2 is Superior: Because PC1 and PC2 are overwhelmingly strong, larger values of mtry (such as 12 or 20) almost always include PC1 or PC2 at every split, making all 1,000 trees nearly identical. Setting mtry = 2 forces trees to frequently evaluate lower-order components (PCs 3–7), creating a much more decorrelated ensemble of trees whose collective majority vote achieves superior accuracy.

2c. Test Evaluation & Confusion Matrix

The selected model (mtry = 2, nmin = 5) was applied to the 317 independent test observations. Test labels were used strictly for this final assessment. Table 6 reports the resulting test confusion matrix.

Table 6: Confusion Matrix on Test Data (Selected Model: mtry = 2, nmin = 5)
Observed True Digit Predicted Digit Total Observed Class Accuracy
Digit 1 Digit 6 Digit 7
Digit 1 102 0 2 104 98.08%
Digit 6 0 106 0 106 100.00%
Digit 7 1 1 105 107 98.13%
Total Predicted 103 107 107 317 Overall: 98.74%
Final Test Performance Summary:
• Total Test Errors: Only 4 errors out of 317 test observations.
• Test Misclassification Rate: 0.0126 (1.26%), corresponding to an overall test accuracy of 98.74%.
• Digit-Level Breakdown: Digit 6 was classified with 100% precision and 100% recall (106/106 correct). Two digit 1s were misclassified as 7s, one digit 7 was misclassified as 1, and one digit 7 was misclassified as 6.
• Comparison to Default: The un-tuned default model (mtry = 6, nmin = 5) incurred 6 test errors (1.89% error rate). Hyperparameter tuning via grid search reduced test errors by 33%, confirming the generalization benefit of tree decorrelation.

Question 3: Planning a Random-Forest Analysis Skill

3a. Design Philosophy & Balancing Instructions

When designing a random-forest analysis skill for an AI agent, the goal is to provide high-level architectural constraints and personal methodological choices without micromanaging standard routine mechanics that a capable model already understands. Because modern LLMs readily comprehend textbook random-forest fundamentals (e.g., recursive binary partitioning, impurity minimization, and bagging), overloading a skill with elementary syntax often causes rigidity, verbosity, or brittle code execution. Instead, the skill should balance standard practices with personal requirements by establishing strict foundational safeguards—such as leak-free data partitioning, fixed pseudo-random seeds, and appropriate candidate parameter grids (mtry spanning $[1, p]$ and terminal node size nmin)—while focusing its primary guidance on user-specific analytical priorities. These personal choices include requiring out-of-bag permutation importance rather than biased Gini impurity metrics, enforcing a strictly budgeted one-page executive summary in 11-point typography, commanding a publication-ready color-blind safe aesthetic (#1b9e77, #d95f02, #7570b3) with embedded base64 graphics, and demanding substantive domain interpretation of feature effects over generic boilerplate. For a capable AI, this division leverages its native statistical competence while reliably steering the final analysis toward the user’s exact methodological, visual, and reporting standards.

3b. 10 Ordered Instructions (from Basic to Personal Preferences)

  1. 1. Problem Formulation & Data Type Validation (Basic Machine Learning) Inspect and validate the input dataset, confirm target variable type (continuous for regression, factor/discrete for classification), encode categorical predictors appropriately, and verify that no missing values exist before fitting.
  2. 2. Strict Data Leakage Prevention (Foundational Methodology) Partition the data into training and held-out test sets prior to any analysis; fit all preprocessing transformations (e.g., centering, scaling, PCA, or imputation) strictly on training observations and apply identical transformations to test observations without snooping.
  3. 3. Reproducibility Standard (Computational Integrity) Explicitly set, document, and report a fixed pseudo-random seed before generating data splits, bootstrap resamples, or running stochastic forest algorithms.
  4. 4. Ensemble Architecture & Bootstrap Sampling (Algorithmic Core) Construct random forests with at least 500 to 1,000 trees to ensure asymptotic variance stabilization, drawing bootstrap samples of size \(N\) with replacement (\(n_{\text{sub}} = N\)) for each individual tree.
  5. 5. Systematic Hyperparameter Tuning Grid (Model Optimization) Tune candidate splitting predictors (mtry) across a wide range (including \(\lfloor\sqrt{p}\rfloor\), \(p/3\), and boundary values) and terminal node size (nmin), comparing candidate settings using out-of-bag (OOB) misclassification rate or cross-validation rather than in-sample training error.
  6. 6. Diagnostic Error Reporting (Statistical Diagnostics) Report both individual tree out-of-bag error and the aggregated ensemble out-of-bag prediction error, providing a complete confusion matrix and per-class error breakdown for classification.
  7. 7. Permutation-Based Variable Importance (Feature Attribution Preference) Quantify predictor importance using out-of-bag permutation feature importance (mean decrease in accuracy/MSE) rather than split-based Gini impurity decrease to prevent bias toward continuous or high-cardinality features.
  8. 8. Clean Table Presentation & Formatting (Stylistic Preference) Present hyperparameter tuning grids, confusion matrices, and ranked feature importances in clean, high-contrast HTML/Markdown tables with the optimal configuration highlighted and numerical values formatted to 3–4 decimal places.
  9. 9. Publication-Quality Plot Aesthetic (Visual Preference) Produce self-contained 7 × 4.5 inch diagnostic plots with clean sans-serif typography (Helvetica/Inter), color-blind safe palettes (#1b9e77, #d95f02, #7570b3), subtle gridlines (#e0e0e0), and embedded data URIs or inline SVGs following STAT 432 visual guidelines.
  10. 10. One-Page Executive Synthesis & Limitation Critique (Personal Reporting Standard) Summarize the final model findings in an executive report strictly constrained to at most one printed page (11-point font), discussing the geometric or substantive interpretation of the top-ranked features, practical trade-offs of the chosen tuning parameters, and explicit analytical limitations.
